Documentary cinema. Filmmaking that purports to record reality rather than fiction—to document actual events, people, and places. Unlike narrative cinema, documentary claims a relationship to truth, and its ethics revolve around the question of what it means to represent reality on film. Documentary has been used for propaganda, journalism, artistic expression, and historical record, often simultaneously, making it one of cinema's most morally complex forms.

The Lumière brothers, Louis and Auguste Lumière, pioneered documentary by filming everyday scenes in the eighteen nineties—workers leaving a factory, a train arriving—and established the observational mode.

Documentary's founding claim is indexicality. Film captures light reflected from the actual world, creating a mechanical trace of reality. This distinguishes it from all other arts, but does not make it objective.

Editing is documentary's invisible hand. Selection, sequencing, and framing determine what is emphasized, omitted, and suggested. No documentary is unmediated reality.

Propaganda documentaries have been influential. Frank Capra directed U.S. Army films during World War II that shaped American understanding of the war. Fascist regimes used documentary to promote ideology.

Observational cinema, also called cinéma vérité, emerged mid-twentieth century and attempted to document without intervention, letting events unfold before the camera. Though the presence of the camera always affects what is filmed.

Documentary encompasses diverse forms: newsreels—brief topical films shown in theaters—educational films, personal essay films, investigative journalism, and artistic or experimental work.

The question of truth in documentary remains unsettled. Film can lie through selection, framing, and juxtaposition even when each image is factually accurate.
